e: Introduction to Characterology By Ludwig Klages Müller & Kiepenheuer Verlag, Potsdam, and Orell Füssli Verlag, Zürich Since an introduction to characterology cannot unfold characterology in its full breadth — even if the space available did not in any case forbid it — it seems fitting to state beforehand what principles guided the author in selecting the material. e: [p. 11] One will answer the question posed in the heading by saying that to characterize means to describe a character. But since this requires concepts of character-traits, the further question arises: what are character-traits? Before we decide this, let us ward off the misunderstanding, which keeps recurring from time to time, that traits are parts of the state of affairs that bears them. According to the teachings of so-called phrenology, for instance, there were supposed to be numerous "faculties" — a sense for thievery, a sense for calculation, a sense for music — corresponding to different regions of the brain and therefore legible from the shape of the skull. That, however, could hold true only for parts of the interpreted facts. But a trait is never a part of its substrate; it is a side of it.

We leave it an open question whether, on some way of looking at things, something truly being-like and alive might really pertain to any state of affairs whatever; for there is no doubt that by a "science of characters" we mean the characters of organic individual beings, which are called, in the borrowed term, "individuals." Individuum comes from in- (un-) and dividuum (divisible), and would thus mean, in literal translation, "the indivisible" (in Greek: atomon). Therein lies a profound insight of language. For if things, one and all, can be divided, it belongs to the nature of the living individual being to be indivisible in at least one respect. I can indeed cut a plant to pieces, or amputate a leg from an animal or a human being; but in doing so I do not likewise cut to pieces the unit of life of the plant, the animal, the human being. Even the single-celled organism, when it doubles itself by division, has thereby transformed itself, just as surely, into two units of life, each of which is in turn capable of doubling itself again.

We translate individuum as individual being, and thereby express that it is the aliveness peculiar to it in respect of which it cannot be divided. To be sure, every transient change of the living body is accompanied by a transient, and every lasting change by a lasting, change of the soul, and, strictly speaking, the reverse holds too; but whereas, for instance, every mutilation — say, castration — by severing an organ from it, also divides the body, at least in part, the polar change of the soul, and hence of its character, that belongs with it is always of a purely qualitative nature and not in the remotest way comparable to a cutting-to-pieces. For historical man, whom we chiefly have in mind, such a mark has long since been recognized: he alone, of all beings, has I-consciousness, and he alone is therefore called a person. Accordingly the human character, or personality, would have to be defined as the individual self, and characterology would have to do with the traits of personal individual beings2. With this we have, for the purposes of scientific inquiry, rejected a narrower sense of the word character on the one hand and of the word personality on the other, but we do not therefore wish to let slip the pointers that this narrower sense is able to give. e: As is well known, there has been much dispute over whether character is innate or acquired. Some maintain its innateness, others its acquiredness, still others let it consist of traits partly innate, partly acquired. The dispute collapses once one reflects clearly on the content of the word "character-trait." If I investigate the character of a thirty-year-old man, the traits peculiar to him are of very different degrees of originality, and there is not the slightest doubt that I would find partly different traits had their bearer grown up, say from his third year of life on, under environmental influences as opposite as possible3. But if I now examine two thirtyyear-old men — twins, say — whose environmental influences, from the first day of their life, were as similar to one another as possible, it is not excluded that I should nonetheless encounter two extraordinarily different characters.

Das Freudegefühl des Forschers über die endlich geglückte Lösung eines lange vergebens umworbenen Problems ist vorwiegend geistiger Natur, das Wehmutsgefühl beim Gedanken an das verlorene Paradies der Kindheit vorwiegend seelischer Natur; weshalb es in beiden Fällen bisweilen Schwierigkeiten bereitet, die auch solchen Gefühlen anhaftenden Umstimmungen des Körpers zu ermitteln. Here, to be sure, the intimacy of the connection between soul and body differs for the various feelings, and one can without difficulty mark off from one another: predominantly sensuous, predominantly psychic, and predominantly spiritual feelings. The researcher's feeling of joy over the finally successful solution of a problem long wooed in vain is of predominantly spiritual nature; the feeling of wistfulness at the thought of the lost paradise of childhood is of predominantly psychic nature; wherefore in both cases it sometimes presents difficulties to ascertain the alterations of the body that cling to such feelings too. The feeling of hunger or of thirst, by contrast, is so very much of a sensuous nature that its mood-character is not seldom drowned out by internal bodily sensations.

e: — Yet such complications do not prevent us from attending to each of the various sides of the life-process on its own, just as we also have to attend to the various sides of character on their own, provided we are minded to investigate character. Here, then, we are concerned exclusively with the feelings. In any feeling whatever, for example the one just already cited, that of hunger, intensity or strength stands out against quality or nature. We feel more or less hunger, more or less thirst — that is, we perform, on two qualitatively (= innature) different feelings, one and the same grading of their strength, thereby clearly distinguishing this from the feeling- "colours" or feeling-"tones." This may at once instruct us concerning the much-disputed difference between feelings and surges of emotion (also called "affects" or "emotions"). Every feeling becomes a surge of emotion the more its colour recedes behind its strength; every surge of emotion becomes a feeling the more its strength recedes behind the colour, to which we shall henceforth give the name "mood." Where mood predominates in a feeling, we speak simply of feelings;

Feelings in the narrower sense, or moods, would accordingly be: for example, low spirits, grief, exhaustion, discontent, cheerfulness; surges of emotion would be: for example, fright, consternation, surprise, an overflow of joy, anger. From words like surge of emotion or emotion [Gemütsbewegung] we hear, as it were, directly what the intensity of feeling actually amounts to. For inner states are thereby named with the help of their coming to light in movements of the living body. Now since a movement-impulse underlies bodily movement, it is evidently the strength of the impulse that we have in view when we speak of violent surges of emotion. Every feeling is qualitatively distinctive thanks to the peculiarity of its mood, and every feeling can be graded by degrees of intensity thanks to the increasability of an impulse inseparable from it. From this it follows, in the first place, that the impulse-side of feeling too partakes in the mood of feeling; for in the urge to annihilate something different is felt than in the urge to unite. For just as, at equal luminosity, we can distinguish degrees of saturation in the quality of red, so too, in two mood-colours, degrees of depth. Beside deep feelings there are shallow feelings, and everyone can recall that he experienced now deep, now shallow, feelings, even if he should designate the feelings experienced by one and the same name. Beside deep inclination stands shallow inclination, deep anger beside shallow anger, deep pleasure beside shallow pleasure. Feelings differing wholly in nature, moreover, not seldom differ quite extraordinarily as to their degree of depth. The highly characteristic state of impatience, or of curiosity, or of boredom, will never attain the depth of mood that the state of longing, or of wistfulness, or of renunciation can at least attain. For those still unpractised in systematic self-reflection, we shall clarify this by setting strength and depth side by side.

e: A deep feeling can at once be violently stirred but also little stirred; a violent surge of emotion at once deeply upheaving, but also extremely shallow. No one will ascribe depth to the violent vexation he had to undergo; no one will call his deep being-moved at the sight of the glowing red evening sun sinking into the sea a violent agitation — whereas the stormy feeling of happiness of two lovers finding each other again after a long separation displays depth and violence together. — Finally, let it be mentioned that, for reasons belonging to the philosophy of language, whose discussion would lead too far here, "depth" occurs in numerous cases as synonymous with "height." "Deep enthusiasm" means essentially the same as "high enthusiasm," "deep joy" as "high joy," "deep veneration" as "high veneration."

The failure to distinguish drives from interests is a chief source of numerous inadequacies in contemporary psychology, and especially of the fruitlessness of its attempts at a science of character. That the two words mean different things admits of no doubt. Granted, then, that we agree to render "interest" in German as "mainspring," drives and mainsprings are different from one another. Insofar as the human being too belongs among the animals, he has drives as they do; insofar as he is, besides, an I-being, he has, alongside these, mainsprings or interests. To the question of what drives are, the answer, if not exhaustive, is at least sufficient: vital causes of movement (= causes of vital movements). Even had what is essential for us not already been supplied in the previous chapter, it would go beyond the scope of an introduction to set forth at length in what respect vital movement differs from mechanical movement. Moreover, the wholly indispensable minimum that we must present is already something decisive. Mechanical movements occur thanks to an impelling "force"; in the context of the organism, by contrast, such "forces" are always determined by a goal. If a tile falls from a roof, this happens out of the "force

But if a thirsting animal sets itself in motion in order to find a watering-place, it is the goal — namely, union with the water through the act of drinking — that has occasioned the movement. And it is always the same in like manner. If, for instance, the stag pursued by the huntsmen flees, he is striving to escape the huntsmen. One must only take care not to confuse the goal-determinateness, which no vital movement lacks, with knowledge of the goal. Have we not seen, in the previous chapter, that every feeling has a stirring proper to it whose direction is to be understood only from the goal! When the storks set out in autumn from East Prussia for Africa, no phantasm of the future settlingplaces hovers before them; rather, they merely follow the awakening migratory drive — which, however, has no less a characteristic goal than thirst has its goal in the drinking of water.

Auch der Mensch, wie bemerkt, hat Triebe; aber sie sind seinen Triebfedern derart untergeordnet, daß sie sich durchweg erst mit deren Hilfe verwirklichen können. — Wir wollen einmal annehmen, es erhöbe hier jemand zum vorhinaus folgenden Einwand: im vorigen Kapitel
e: We may also put it this way: the drive is, among other things, felt privation-suffering, and this has the peculiar gift of developing out of itself movements that find their end in the removal of the privation. It follows from this that we already think the word 'cause' differently than physics does. Mechanical causes are (calculable) conditions for the occurrence of an event; vital causes, by contrast, are producing causes. The concept of the producing cause was created by antiquity; the concept of cause as mere condition was created by the modern age, in the wake of Galileo and Newton. If one asks how vital (= producing) causes are possible at all, the remark must suffice here that they point back to connections between the soul of the individual being and the images of the world. Man too, as noted, has drives; but these are so subordinated to his mainsprings that they can, throughout, be realized only with the latter's help. — Let us assume that someone raised here, in anticipation, the following objection: in the

We answer: because in countless cases man, and only man, arrives at the fulfilling goal of his stirring no longer directly but only indirectly, namely by the detour of willing. Almost all the further expositions that follow will serve at once as a more exact elucidation of this sentence, whose grounding we for now only prepare. The conceptual definition of the mainspring runs: mainsprings are causes of will. But since what matters here is not the magnitude of the exertion of will, not the ease or difficulty of the decision, nor equally that of its execution — all of which would be matters of aptitude — but solely the decisive goal, one says more precisely: every mainspring is the dispositional condition of a direction of will. e: different from a cause of movement. Whenever the attempt has hitherto been made to interpret the will, the analogy of the cause of movement has always hovered before the mind, and the consequence of this was that, down to the present day, no doctrine of the will could arise. The achievement of the will is to set purposes and to hold fast, in the direction of the purpose, a life of movement available to it. Just as it is by no means the sergeant's marching order that sets the soldier's legs in motion, but rather his 'living force', so likewise it is not the inner command (namely, of the will) but an effective driving force of vitality by which action comes about; and just as the marching order does indeed show the marching soldier the direction, so exactly does the inner command bind the impulsive movement to a punctual goal, which stems from it no more than the marching order stems from the soldier's will. It is no accident that the word 'Zweck' [purpose], which originally meant the peg at the centre of the target, has come to designate exclusively the goal of the will! Far from generating movements, the will acts upon an impulsive movement that has been deprived of its natural goal, steering or regulating it by binding it to the direction of the now 'prescribed' purpose. How is this possible? It is possible only because a new power enters into the nexus of individual life — namely that power through which it becomes an I-being: its name is spirit. All that lives is ensouled; but man alone is, in addition, spirited — or, more precisely, only historical man, including the immediately prehistoric segment of his unhistorical existence. Spirit stands in such opposition to life that it acts, under all circumstances, at least restrictively upon life's unfolding. Let a simile make this

o: uns ein Gleichnis anschaulich machen. Wir vergleichen die Triebe einer lodernden Flamme, die leuchtet und Wärme verbreitet. Soll sie nun eine Maschine treiben, so müssen wir zunächst einmal die Maschine bauen und ferner dafür Sorge 1ragen, daß die Wärmeausströmung der Flamme eingeengt und möglichst vollständig zur Erwärmung des Wassers im Kessel verwertet wird. Denken wir noch hinzu (womit das Gleichnis freilich gesprengt wird), auch die Maschine sei irgendwie aus der Wärme des Feuers gewonnen, so entspräche sie völlig dem lebengekoppelten Geiste, dessen Wirkung auf die Triebe folglich darin bestände, einen Teil ihrer Energie zur Regelung des andern Teils zu verbrauchen behufs Verwirklichung des gedanklichen Zweckes. Soweit das tatsächlich geschieht, sprechen wir nicht mehr von Trieben, sondern von Triebfedern oder Interessen und nicht mehr von triebhaften Impulsen, sondern von planmäßigen Willensakten. — Das Beispiel der Maschine mag uns gleich noch den Zusatz „planmäßig“ aufhellen. Die Flamme lodert und leuchtet und wärmt; aber nur, soweit sie den Kessel heizt, ist sie imstande, wenigstens mittelbar, nämlich mit Hilfe der Maschine, unzähligemale
e: vivid too. We compare the drives to a blazing flame that gives light and spreads warmth. If it is now to drive a machine, we must first build the machine and further see to it that the flame's outflow of heat is confined and used as completely as possible to warm the water in the boiler. If we add further (with which, admittedly, the simile is sprung) that the machine too was somehow won from the fire's heat, it would correspond entirely to the life-coupled spirit, whose effect on the drives would consequently consist in expending part of their energy to regulate the other part, for the sake of realizing the conceptual purpose. Insofar as this actually happens, we no longer speak of drives but of mainsprings or interests, and no longer of driven impulses but of purposeful acts of will. — The example of the machine may at once clarify the addition 'purposeful' for us. The flame blazes and shines and warms; but only insofar as it heats the boiler is it capable — at least indirectly, that is, with the machine's help — of performing,

o: eine und dieselbe Arbeit zu leisten. Triebe regen sich, wachsen, befriedigen sich und klingen ab, sei es auf Eindrücke hin, sei es aus inneren ‚Reizen‘; nur aber der Teil von ihnen, der in die Botmäßigkeit des Willens geriet und dadurch in ein Interesse verwandelt wurde, arbeitet Jahre und selbst Jahrzehnte lang an der Erreichung des einen und selben Zweckes. Ein Tier kann flüchten, Nahrung suchen, Wintervorräte aufspeichern, Eier bebrüten, Tausende von Kilometern durchmessen: seine Bewegungen und Verhaltungen sind gleichwohl immer so unmittelbar wie möglich auf das seiner Regung innewohnende Ziel gerichtet. Was aber kein Tier, was ausschließlich der willensbebefähigte Mensch vermag, ist: Bewegungen auszuführen, die nur der Ermöglichung andrer Bewegungen dienen, von denen dasselbe gilt, und so durch eine unübersehliche Reihe von Zwischengliedern hindurch bis zum weit in der Zukunft liegenden Zweck. Ein junger Mann tritt mittellos als Lehrling in ein Geschäft mit dem brennenden Wounsche, selbst Geschäftsinhaber zu werden. Ein Jahrzehnt mag vergehen und länger, bis
e: countless times, one and the same piece of work. Drives stir, grow, satisfy themselves and die away, whether in response to impressions or out of inner 'stimuli'; but only that part of them which has fallen under the sway of the will, and has thereby been transformed into an interest, works for years and even decades toward the attainment of one and the same purpose. An animal can flee, seek food, store up winter provisions, brood its eggs, traverse thousands of kilometres: its movements and behaviours are nevertheless always directed as immediately as possible toward the goal inherent in its stirring. But what no animal, and only will-endowed man, is capable of, is this: to carry out movements that serve only to make possible other movements, of which the same holds true, and so on through an unsurveyable series of intermediate links all the way to a purpose lying far in the future. A young man enters a business, penniless, as an apprentice, with the burning wish himself to become an owner of the business one day. A decade may pass, or more, before fulfilment

o: ihm Erfüllung wird. Inzwischen hat er tausend und tausend Bewegungen ausgeführt, die, in keinem Zusammenhange mit seinen (vitalen) Trieben stehend, sinnlos wären, hätten sie nicht die Bedeutung von ebenso vielen Mittelgliedern gehabt im Dienste der Verwirklichung eines Entschlusses, der schon am Anfang aller der Jahre feststand! Nur solche Bewegungen tragen mit Recht den Namen der Handlung. Aber damit nicht genug, der Mensch kann Zwecke verfolgen und tut es unzähligemal, deren Verwirklichung weit jenseits der Grenzen seines Lebens liegt. Wenn ein naturliebender Gutsbesitzer, den die Vernichtung der Urwälder schmerzt, ein Servitut errichtet, wonach die Bäume, die er auf einem Landstrich von fünfhundert Morgen anpflanzt, nie geschlagen werden dürfen, so weiß er gewiß, daß er die Stämme von mindestens fünfzig Meter Höhe, deren Verwirklichung er anstrebt, nie zu sehen bekommen wird, sondern allenfalls seine Urenkel. Und wenn ein Staatsmann, der die Vermehrung der Bewohnerschaft des Landes auf das Doppelte plant, im Alter von sechzig Jahren ein Gesetz durchbringt, das für Junggesellen eine hohe Extrasteuer,
e: comes to him. Meanwhile he has carried out a thousand upon a thousand movements which, standing in no connection with his (vital) drives, would have been senseless had they not had the significance of just as many intermediate links in the service of realizing a resolve that stood fixed already at the beginning of all those years! Only such movements rightly bear the name of action. But that is not all: man can pursue purposes, and does so countless times, whose realization lies far beyond the bounds of his own life. When a nature-loving landowner, pained by the destruction of the primeval forests, establishes an easement providing that the trees he plants on a tract of five hundred acres may never be felled, he certainly knows that he himself will never get to see the trunks of at least fifty metres' height whose realization he is striving for, but at most his great-grandchildren will. And when a statesman who plans to double the population of the country pushes through, at the age of sixty, a law that fixes a

o: für alle Familien mit mehr als fünf Kindern aber eine Prämie bestimmt, so weıß er ebenfalls, daß erst kommende Geschlechter von seiner Maßnahme die Folgen erleben werden. Über welche Zeıtenfluchten vollends spannen bewußt den Bogen ihres Willens große Religionsstifter, ob ihre „Gemeinde“ gleich während ihres Lebens eine verschwindende Minderheit bilde und noch dazu meist innerhalb einer Zeitgenossenschaft, die auf den Neuerer und seine Jüngerschar gewöhnlich mit Hohn und Verachtung herabblickt7I Sollte man es angesichts dessen für möglich halten, daß die Ursache der Handlung, d. i. die Triebfeder, mit der Ursache der Antriebsbewegung, d. i. dem Triebe, jemals konnte verwechselt werden!
e: high extra tax for bachelors but a bonus for all families with more than five children, he likewise knows that only coming generations will experience the consequences of his measure. Over what stretches of time, finally, do great founders of religions consciously span the bow of their will, even though their "community", during their own lifetime, forms a vanishing minority, and that too mostly within a contemporary society that usually looks down with scorn and contempt on the innovator and his band of disciples7 Should one, in view of all this, consider it possible that the cause of action, that is, the mainspring, could ever have been confused with the cause of the impulsive movement, that is, the drive!

o: Goethes Faust, im Begriffe, die ‚Heilige Schrift‘ zu übertragen, gerät in Zweifel über die Bedeutung schon ihres ersten Satzes, um nach mehreren Versuchen, die ihn nicht recht befriedigen, entschlossen niederzuschreiben: im Anfang war die Tat. Im Einklange damit läßt der mosaische Schöpfungsmythos die Welt aus dem Nichts hervorgerufen werden durch den Befehl eines Gottes. Niemals hat es ein Mensch erlebt, und niemals wird es ein Mensch erleben, daß ein Kommando ohne Beihilfe anderweitig verfügbarer Mächte einen Stein zu bewegen, geschweige ihn zu schaffen vermöchte; und am „Anfange‘“ war gewiß nicht die Tat, weil ein lebendiger und sogar ein begeisteter Körper vorhanden sein muß, damit
e: Goethe's Faust, engaged in translating the 'Holy Scripture', falls into doubt over the meaning of even its first sentence, until, after several attempts that do not quite satisfy him, he resolves to write down: In the beginning was the deed. In keeping with this, the Mosaic creation myth has the world called forth out of nothing by the command of a God. Never has a man experienced, and never will a man experience, that a command, without the assistance of otherwise available powers, could move a stone, let alone create it; and at the "beginning" it was certainly not the deed, because a living and even a spirited body must be present before a deed

o: eine Tat vollbracht werden könne. Gleichwohl haben beide Daten, der mosaische Schöpfungsmythos und Fausts Übertragungsanhub, eine tiefsinnige Bedeutung, die erstmals erschlossen wurde von jenen mittelalterlichen Interpreten der Kirchendogmen, die im äußersten Gegensatz zur Denkweise des gesamten Altertums den Geist als „reine Tat‘ definierten und demgemäß sein Wesen nicht im Intellekt, sondern im Willen zu finden vermeinten8. Seither hat sich immer entschiedener eine Psychologie der ‚Akte‘ entwickelt, wenn auch erst ein einziger Denker imstande war, der ihr innewohnenden Tendenz die erfüllende Entdeckung hinzuzufügen9. Nicht an dieser Stelle können wir eine Untersuchung des Wesens der Akte bieten; aber auch ohne sie dürfte verständlich10 werden, was wir davon für die Charakterkunde benötigen. — Es gibt zwei echte Akte, nicht mehr und nicht weniger, den Auffassungsakt und den Willensakt. Es muß nun wenigstens ein Auffassungsakt stattgefunden haben, damit ein Willensakt stattfinden könne; aber nur aus diesem, darin hatten jene Scholastiker recht, ermitteln wir das Wesen der geistigen Tat überhaupt. Betrachten wir zuvörderst die
e: can be accomplished. All the same, both these data — the Mosaic creation myth and the beginning of Faust's translation — have a profound meaning, one first disclosed by those medieval interpreters of church dogma who, in the sharpest opposition to the whole mode of thought of antiquity, defined spirit as "pure act" and accordingly supposed its essence to be found not in the intellect but in the will8. Since then a psychology of 'acts' has developed ever more decisively, even though only a single thinker so far has been able to add to its inherent tendency the fulfilling discovery9. This is not the place to offer an investigation of the nature of acts ; but even10 without it, what we need from this for characterology should become intelligible. — There are two genuine acts, no more and no fewer: the act of apprehension and the act of will. Now at least one act of apprehension must have taken place for an act of will to take place; but it is only from this act — and here those Scholastics were right — that we ascertain the nature of the spiritual deed as such. Let us consider first of all

o: ursprünglichste Form des Auffassungsaktes, den Wahrnehmungsakt, und setzen wir den Fall, der Wahrnehmungsgegenstand dränge sich uns auf, so sind wir zweifellos außerstande, etwas einer Tätigkeit Ähnliches in uns festzustellen. Wer beim Spazierengehen über einen vorspringenden Pflasterstein stolpert und ihn infolgedessen wohl oder übel bemerken muß, dem ist seine Wahrnehmung so sehr abgenötigt, daß er es sicher bestritte, wollte man ihm vordemonstrieren, es habe zu solchem Bemerken einer Tat seines Geistes bedurft. Und wer sich — gemäß einer heute glücklicherweise im Schwinden begriffenen Unmethode — darauf versteifte, von seelischen und geistigen Sachverhalten nur zuzugeben, was er vermöge sogenannter Selbstbeobachtung oder Innenschau zu erhaschen vermöchte, der würde von der Tatnatur seiner Auffassungsvorgänge wahrscheinlich niemals zu überzeugen sein. Bevor wir zeigen, daß es dennoch ein Mittel gibt, seine Umstimmung vorzubereiten, betrachten wir eine, wenn nicht notwendige, so doch jederzeit mögliche Folge des Auffassungsaktes.
e: the most original form of the act of apprehension, the act of perception, and let us suppose the case that the object of perception forces itself upon us; then we are undoubtedly unable to establish in ourselves anything resembling an activity. Whoever, out for a walk, stumbles over a jutting pavingstone and is consequently forced, willy-nilly, to notice it, has his perception so thoroughly extorted from him that he would certainly dispute it, were one to try to demonstrate to him that such noticing had required a deed of his spirit. And whoever — following an unmethod that is happily on the wane today — insisted on admitting, of psychic and spiritual states of affairs, only what he could seize by means of so-called selfobservation or introspection, would probably never be convinced of the act-nature of his processes of apprehension. Before we show that there is nevertheless a means of preparing his change of mind, let us consider a consequence of the act of apprehension that is, if not necessary, at least always possible.

o: So oft ich etwas auffasse, kann ich das Aufgefaßte stempeln, indem ich darüber ein Urteil fälle. Wahrnehme ich etwas Helles, so kann ich mindestens urteilen: da ist etwas Helles; wahrnehme ich genauer ein Licht, so etwa: da ist ein Licht; wahrnehme ich noch genauer, so etwa: da ist eine Stehlampe. Urteile sind innere Handlungen, die in äußern Handlungen sich entladen können, sei es durch sprachliche Verlautbarung, sei es durch sonstige Zeichengebung;; Handlungen aber setzen Wollungen voraus; und die Wollung ist nach dem Zeugnis unmittelbarer Selbstbesinnung eine Tätigkeit des Ichs. Uns beschäftigt hier nicht das Verhältnis der Urteilshandlung zum Auffassungsakt; aber wir überlegen uns, daß schon ihre Möglichkeit uns belehrt, es werde im Moment des Erfassens etwas von uns geleistet. Es soll uns dabei nicht kümmern, daß unser Spaziergänger, wann er ärgerlich ausruft: „Dieses elende Pflaster bedürfte dringend der Aufbesserung!'‘, den Begriff des Pflasters, den Begriff von Steinen, Begriffe zahlreicher Eigenschaften der Steine schon hat; es sollen uns ebensowenig die mancherlei Empfindungsvorgänge kümmern, auf die man zum Behuf der Erklärung von Wahrnehmungsinhalten
e: Whenever I apprehend something, I can stamp what has been apprehended, by passing a judgment on it. If I perceive something bright, I can at least judge: there is something bright; if I perceive more precisely a light, then, say: there is a light; if I perceive still more precisely, then, say: there is a standing lamp. Judgments are inner actions that can discharge themselves in outer actions, whether through verbal utterance or through some other giving of signs; but actions presuppose volitions, and volition, on the testimony of immediate self-reflection, is an activity of the I. We are not concerned here with the relation of the act of judging to the act of apprehension; but we consider that its very possibility already teaches us that something is being accomplished by us in the moment of grasping. It need not trouble us here that our walker, when he exclaims in annoyance, "This wretched pavement badly needs repair!", already has the concept of the pavement, the concept of stones, the concepts of numerous properties of stones; just as little need the manifold processes of sensation

o: zurückzugreifen pflegt, und nur auf das eine legen wir Gewicht, daß man dem Pflasterstein, an dem man sich gestoßen, mit dem Urteil darüber unfehlbar Existenz beimißt; denn nur dieses eine gilt ohne Ausnahme von jedem beliebigen Wahrnehmungsgegenstande, mag er übrigens wıe immer beschaffen sein, und eben dies eine liegt nie und nimmer im Widerfahrnis der Erscheinung des Steines. Gesetzt, es verhielte sıch so, dann muß ein Etwas in uns bereits im Moment des Erfassens die Existenz zur Erscheinung hinzugebracht haben und mithin tätig gewesen sein, ob auch der Auffassungsträger nicht das geringste davon bemerkt hat. Nun, dies Tätige ist dasselbige Etwas, dessen Tätigsein uns bewußt wird, so oft wir Entschlüsse fassen, Entscheidungen treffen, uns widersetzen, selbsttätig anspannen, anstrengen, kürzer, so oft wir wollen. Vielleicht entgegnet man — und größte Denker der Vergangenheit, wenn auch nicht alle, schlössen sich an —, in der Erscheinung des Steines liege doch auch das Existieren des Steines; aber dann hätte man Existenz mit Wirklichkeit verwechselt!
e: trouble us, to which one is accustomed to have recourse for the sake of explaining the contents of perception, and we lay weight on this one point alone: that one infallibly attributes existence, in the judgment made about it, to the pavingstone against which one has struck oneself; for this one point alone holds without exception of any object of perception whatsoever, however it may otherwise be constituted, and this very point never lies, not ever, in the mere happening-to-one of the stone's appearance. Supposing this to be so, then something in us must already, in the moment of grasping, have added existence to the appearance, and must therefore have been active, even though the bearer of the apprehension noticed nothing of it whatsoever. Now, this active something is the selfsame something whose being-active becomes conscious to us as often as we form resolves, make decisions, resist, exert and strain ourselves spontaneously — in short, as often as we will. Perhaps one will object — and the greatest thinkers of the past, though not all, have joined in this — that in the appearance

o: Die Erscheinung des Steines wird als etwas Wirkliches erlebt, und das bedeutet genauer als etwas der Wirklichkeit des Erlebenden Fremdes. Wir fragen, ob es deshalb und deshalb allein schon etwas Existierendes sei. — Wir denken nıchts Wirkliches, ohne es als zeitlich wirklich zu denken. Versuchen wir jetzt, uns nur ein wenig in das zu vertiefen, was „Zeitlichkeit‘“ meine, so wird es uns nicht entgehen, daß, was uns dabei wohl zunächst sich aufdrängen will, die streckenmäßig in Sekunden teılbare Zeit, von uns selber, falls eine kühnere Wendung erlaubt ist, erfunden wurde zwecks geistiger Aneignung des sonst unfaßlichen Sachverhalts eines niemals pausierenden Fliehens der Welterscheinung. Die Zeit als solche hat ja doch keine Einschnitte und Stellen. Nun aber besinne man sich: nur dadurch, daß wir etwas Erscheinendes mit Stellen der Zeit in Verbindung bringen, wird es zum Existierenden, und das will sagen, zu jenem ganz neuartig Wirklichen, auf das wir zu jeder beliebigen Zeit denkend zurückgreifen können als auf etwas (für immer) mit sich Identisches. Ob wir dabei etwas derartiges im Auge haben, das sich wie
e: of the stone the existence of the stone is also already contained; but then one would have confused existence with actuality! The appearance of the stone is experienced as something actual, and this means, more precisely, as something foreign to the actuality of the one experiencing it. We ask whether it is, for that reason and that reason alone, already something existing. — We think nothing actual without thinking it as temporally actual. If we now try to sink ourselves a little into what "temporality" means, it will not escape us that what first presses itself upon us here — time divisible, stretch-wise, into seconds — was, if a bolder turn of phrase is allowed, invented by ourselves for the sake of the spiritual appropriation of the otherwise ungraspable state of affairs of a never-pausing flight of world-appearance. Time as such has, after all, no incisions and no positions. But now let one consider: only by our bringing something appearing into connection with positions in time does it become something existing — and that is to say, that wholly new kind of actual thing to which we can, thinkingly, have recourse at any time whatever, as to something (forever) identical with itself. Whether we have in mind something of the sort that, like the pavingstone,

o: der Pflasterstein auch körperlich wiederfinden no läßt, oder etwas erscheinungsmäßig so ungemein Flüchtiges wie den Blitz, ändert am hier ermittelten Sachverhalt nichts. Urteile ich nämlich „es hat geblitzt‘“ (etwa vor fünf Minuten; oder auch gestern abend), so behaupte ich das Vorhandensein des Blitzes an einer jetzt freilich verflossenen Stelle der Zeit; ebenso mit dem Urteil, daß dann und dann etwas stattfinden werde, Analoges durch Bezugnahme auf cine erst zu erwartenden Stelle der Zeit. Weit entfernt, Bewußtsein der Wirklichkeit zu sein, ist Existenzbewußtsein die Kehrseite eines Zeitbewußtseins, das dem unaufhaltsamen Flüchten der Welterscheinung die beliebig verlängerbare Strecke unterstellt hat, auf deren (fiktive) Stellen wir die Erscheinung zwangsmäßig beziehen. Hat aber dergestalt unser Auffassungsvermögen das schon geleistet, was unser Urteil darüber uns nur zum Bewußtsein bringt, so hat es im Auffassungsaugenblick eine Tat vollbracht, von welcher der Auffassungsträger allerdings nichts bemerkte, weil er — aus hier zu weit führenden Gründen — vom Ergebnis der Tat gefesselt war und nicht gleichzeitig das Tun zu beachten vermochte.
e: can also be found again bodily, or something as extraordinarily fleeting in its appearance as lightning, changes nothing in the state of affairs here ascertained. For if I judge "it has lightninged" (say, five minutes ago, or last evening), I assert the presence of the lightning-flash at a position of time that has, admittedly, now elapsed; and likewise with the judgment that such-and-such will take place then and there — analogously, by reference to a position of time still to be expected. Far from being consciousness of actuality, existence-consciousness is the reverse side of a time-consciousness that has laid the arbitrarily extendable stretch beneath the unstoppable flight of world-appearance, onto whose (fictive) positions we compulsorily refer the appearance. But if our faculty of apprehension has, in this way, already accomplished what our judgment about it merely brings to consciousness for us, then it has, in the moment of apprehension, accomplished a deed of which the bearer of the apprehension nonetheless noticed nothing, because he — for reasons that would lead too far afield here — was held captive by the result of the deed and was unable, at the same time, to attend to the doing.

o: Das Tier lebt wie wir in einer Wirklichkeit, bald vornehmlich von Geruchserscheinungen, bald mehr von Gehörs-und Gesichtserscheinungen, grundsätzlich immer von Tasterscheinungen und somit zumal in einer Wirklichkeit der Körper; aber kein Tier lebt gleich uns in einer Wirklichkeit von Existenzen oder Dingen; denn kein Tier hat Bewußtsein der Zeit11. Aber damit haben wir von der neuen Macht mit Namen Geist, die im Menschen, ihn von der Tierheit trennend, zur Vitalität hinzugekommen, bereits das Wesen herausgefunden. — Sie stellt ihn neben die Zeit, oder denn sie reißt ihn aus der Zeit heraus, indem sie ihm die Zeitlichkeit alles Wirklichen „gegenständlich“, d. i. zu etwas Entgegenstehendem macht und dergestalt das Wirkliche selbst in jenes einzigartige Etwas verwandelt, das inbezug auf die Zeit „existiert“. Sie kann das aber nur deshalb, weil sie in ihn selber eingekehrt ist, fortan den beherrschenden Mittelpunkt seines Wesens bildend, im Verhältnis zu dem der schon vorhandene Mittelpunkt seiner Vitalität mehr oder minder exzentrisch wird; welchen Namen wir bezeichnenderweise dem Unvernünftigen,
e: The animal lives, as we do, in an actuality — now chiefly of olfactory appearances, now more of auditory and visual appearances, but fundamentally always of tactile appearances, and thus above all in an actuality of bodies; but no animal lives, as we do, in an actuality of existences or things; for no animal has consciousness of time11. But with this we have already found the essence of the new power called spirit, which, in man, separating him from animality, has been added to vitality. — It sets him alongside time, or rather it tears him out of time, in that it makes the temporality of everything actual "objective" to him, that is, into something standing over against him, and thereby transforms the actual itself into that singular something which, with respect to time, "exists". But it can do this only because it has taken up residence within him himself, henceforth forming the ruling centre of his being, in relation to which the already existing centre of his vitality becomes more or less eccentric — a name we characteristically tend to attach to the unreasonable, the

o: Unverständigen, im metaphysischen Sinne Unzweckmäßigen anzuheften pflegen. Nennen wir den auf solche Weise mit der Vitalität gekoppelten Geist das persönliche Ich, so haben wir den Sachverhalt angezeigt, der in einer Wirklichkeit des unaufhörlichen Vergehens einzig und allein wirklich existiert, und können durch unmittelbare Rückbesinnung die Probe aufs Exempel machen. Fragt sich nämlich jemand, was er eigentlich meine, wenn er von sich als von einem Ich rede, so findet er nichts als ein schlechthin Existierendes, auf das der Begriff der Veränderung, geschweige der Wandlung, keine Anwendung findet. Auf einen Zeitraum von etwa dreißig Jahren zurückblickend, wird er außerordentlicher Änderungen seines Körpers gewahr, auch der mannigfachsten Änderungen seines Wesens; aber, indem er jedes von beiden, Körper wie Wesen, das seinige nennt, hat er sie beide an ein unwandelbar mit sich identisches Ich geknüpft, das er als eines und immer dasselbe von jedem je gewesenen, seienden und seinwerdenden Ich unterscheidet. ‚Ich‘ war es, der ınit fünf Jahren ins Regenfaß fiel,
e: uncomprehending, the inexpedient in the metaphysical sense. If we call the spirit thus coupled with vitality the personal I, then we have indicated the state of affairs that alone truly exists, in an actuality of unceasing passing-away, and we can put it to the test by immediate reflection back upon ourselves. For if someone asks himself what he actually means when he speaks of himself as an I, he finds nothing but a sheer existent to which the concept of alteration, let alone of transformation, finds no application. Looking back over a span of some thirty years, he becomes aware of extraordinary changes in his body, and also of the most manifold changes in his character; but in calling each of the two, body as well as character, his own, he has tied them both to an I unchangeably identical with itself, which he distinguishes, as one and always the same, from every I that ever was, is, or is becoming. It was 'I'

e: Our characterization of the human feeling-life in accordance with Figure 1 presupposes that both the I and the It are turned toward one another and, precisely for that reason, rival one another. If we seek a mark for it that comprises all its varieties, however different these may otherwise be, we find it most easily through a brief consideration of self-feeling. In accordance with the ceaseless disputes between I and It, all things undergone by the personality, all workings-through of the material of experience, all achievements, and then also all supposed and actual properties, arrange themselves for the personality into the onedimensional graded series of personal values, and are accordingly experienced, at the very least, as either valuable or contrary to value, or finally, at most, as value-indifferent (the adiaphora of the Greeks!) — and by reflective minds even weighed as such. Strictly speaking there is, in the personality, no feeling that would not carry a specific value-coloring attached to it; and it is only with the description of this — including the weighing of its consequent phenomena — that the depiction of the feeling-life is first completed.

Just as the I and the It can strive toward one another like two hostile armies and become locked in combat, so too they can strive apart from one another; and the consequences of this turn out differently for the bearer according to whether his centre of gravity must be located in the I or in the It. If — what concerns us first — the latter is the case, the I-side loses more and more the character of the individual I, and in its place steps the dominion of spirit itself, which after all could only become individual spirit in proportion to its interweaving with life. After the foregoing remarks it will not surprise us that it was a friend and pupil of Aristotle, namely Theophrastus (370–287), who led the peripatetic school after him, to whom we owe the first work of characterology in the most proper sense of the word. Though his thirty "Character Sketches" may be in part reworked and disfigured, they are and remain an ineradicable landmark of thought — even if not only for the good! Theophrastus's procedure — not, to be sure, thought through, but in fact practised — is this: he takes possession of a real or supposed character trait and, by picturing its consequences for overall behaviour (especially in social intercourse), forms out of it a type, which he then, through an astonishingly rich exemplification, transforms back into the most vivid shape. Who would not see before him the "Tactless Man" on hearing: "He is always officiously ready to serve just where one does not want his services and yet can hardly well refuse them"; or the "Miser" at the words: "If his wife has lost a threepenny piece, he is capable of moving aside every piece of household furniture, every bed and cupboard, and shaking

Nie banal, durchweg geistvoll und stets überlegen bietet er nichts, was jeder nicht auch heute noch bestätigen könnte. Allein erhat mit seiner echt griechischen Vereinfachung einen Irrtum gesät, der bis auf weiteres lustig wuchert: den, wie es scheint, unausrottbaren Glauben an das wirkliche Dasein von Typen. Nichts beweist wohl schlagender die Denkabhängigkeit des abendländischen Menschen von den Griechen als der Umstand, daß man von der typologischen Auffassung der Charaktere nicht mehr losgekommen ist24! And in the same breath he boldly asserts that the Asiatic craftsmen are far superior to the European ones — and all this he says without ever having left his native town"! He sketches — in passing, as it were, and without being burdened by learned names — a picture, accurate in its main features, of pseudologia phantastika [fantastic lying], partly in the "Braggart," partly in the "Duck-Hunter," of whom he remarks in conclusion: "They are a strange lot, these duck-hunters, for not only is their whole business nothing but lies and deception, they not infrequently have the loss from it into the bargain as well" (I). Never banal, throughout full of wit, and always superior, he offers nothing that anyone could not confirm even today. Yet, with his genuinely Greek simplification, he sowed an error that continues merrily to proliferate to this day: the, it seems, ineradicable belief in the real existence of types. e: typological conception of characters24! Rightly do the French call the greatest poet of their greatest century the father of their comedy. But what are Molière's characters? Theophrastan types! "Tartuffe," "The Misanthrope," "The Imaginary Invalid," "The Miser," etc. — nothing but properties transformed into persons! Once again put on the stage with wit and with the outstanding knowledge of human nature of the man of the world — truly immortal types! Yet the recipe is always at hand, while wit and knowledge of human nature are not inheritable. The average scholar of today has the recipe; he does not have the wit and the knowledge of human nature, and so he knocks together his types for home use — or rather, unfortunately, not only for home use! (The writer of these lines declares himself willing, should it be absolutely necessary, and then of course only for a corresponding fee, to draft a typology every week — some fifty a year, then, each with a sufficiently persuasive rationale....). — Only in the schools of the Cynics and Cyrenaics does that one-sided individualism develop which places the personality at the centre of actuality, and precisely thereby brings to light, though in a form more epigrammatic than scientific, a good many insights into man. Here are a few sayings (always in Nestle's translation) with which we should like to give the reader a taste for turning to the authors named above. Antisthenes: "One must pay attention to one's enemies, for they are the first to notice our faults." Diogenes: "A drop of luck is worth more than a barrelful of wit"; "The sun, too, shines into corners and yet is not defiled"; "Fame is a noise made by raving men." Crates: "In this man's case, it is not he who possesses the wealth, but the wealth that possesses him." (!) Historically, the Stoa branched off from Cynicism, and Epicureanism from the Hedonism of the Cyrenaics; and with that we are at the center of ancient character research. No one properly understands this who has not thoroughly studied the surviving sayings of at least the following representatives of both schools: Epicurus, Philodemus, Chrysippus, Seneca, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius. If among the later Stoics Marcus Aurelius is the most profound, then Seneca is the most brilliant and characterologically the most productive! The continuers of the Greco-Latin spirit were, as is well known, the French. From the long series of ingenious authors we name only the most indispensable: Montaigne's "Essais," Labruyère's "Les Caractères" (1680), La Rochefoucauld's "Maximes" (1690), and finally Stendhal's "De l'amour." — With the second half of the 18th century the psychological awakening of Germany begins, soon to produce peak achievements that scarcely have their equal. And here we must above all recall two works by poets, each of which, in our estimation, harbors a treasure-house of characterological wisdom unsurpassed in richness — we mean Goethe's "Die Wahlverwandtschaften" and Jean Paul's "Levana," a book which among other things offers the most excellent treatment yet given of the essential difference between the sexes. Seit dem Beginn des 19. Jahrhunderts gabeln sich deutlich zwei Strömungen. Die eine ausgehend von Schopenhauer, der ein weit größerer Seelenkenner als epekulativer Metaphysiker war, hat schließlich das Werk hervorgetrieben, das dem ganzen Wissensgebiet den unterscheidenden Namen lieh, nämlich Bahnsens 1867 erschienenen zweibändigen „Beiträge zur Charakterologie‘, und überdies infolge wunderlicher Vermengung mit den Seelenforschungen Herbarts der heute so genannten Psychoanalyse ihr begriffliches Rüstzeug geliefert. Since the beginning of the 19th century two currents clearly diverge. The one, proceeding from Schopenhauer — who was a far greater knower of the soul than a speculative metaphysician — eventually produced the work that lent the whole field of knowledge its distinguishing name, namely Bahnsen's two-volume "Beiträge zur Charakterologie," published in 1867, and moreover, through a curious mingling with Herbart's researches into the soul, supplied the conceptual apparatus for what is today called psychoanalysis. The other is introduced most magnificently by the thinkers of Romanticism oriented toward psychology and physiognomy. Among the works belonging here, the most important for us today is "Psyche. Zur Entwicklungsgeschichte der Seele" by C. G. Carus (1846, reissued with an introductory preface by Klages at Diederichs, Jena). But Schubert's hymnic "Geschichte der Seele" also greets us across the years as an imperishable monument. In this, however, lies the decisively new element of Romantic psychology: that it seeks the wellspring

Wer heute am Bau der Charakterkunde mitwirken will, der darf sich kein einziges der Bücher Nietzsches erlassen. Als Kompaß zur Durchquerung dieses gefahrdrohenden Feuerregens von Neugedanken empfehlen wir ihm unser Werk „Die psychologischen Errungenschaften Nietzsches (Barth, Leipzig). Hier nur die eine Bemerkung: Nietzsche zeigt, daß Wesenserkenntnis unmöglich ist, es sei denn, wir hätten zuvor sämtliche Selbsttäuschungen durchschaut und aufgelöst, mit denen die seit Jahrtausenden vom Geiste verführte Menschheit sich gegen das Eingeständnis der Lebensschändung gepanzert hat. Er fordert uns auf, Chirurgen unsrer Seele zu werden, und drückt uns das Messer in die Hand, das bis ins Knochenmark des Charakters schneidet. — Zu Nietzsches seelenkundlichen Entdeckungen gesellt sich nun aber, teilweise durch sie gefördert, eine der Mechanistik energisch absatzende Lebenslehre (Biologie), deren weitaus bedeutendster Vertreter, Melchior Palägyi, in seinen „Naturphilosophischen Vorlesungen“ die Scheidung von Geist und Leben streng begrifflich vollendet. — Den vorläufigen Abschluß endlich bietet unser Werk „Die Grundlagen der Charakterkunde‘“. Damit wären wir denn in der
e: every "then" and the "now" steps the revolutionizing creative spirit Friedrich Nietzsche. Whoever today wishes to help build the edifice of characterology may spare himself none of Nietzsche's books. As a compass for traversing this dangerous firestorm of new thoughts we recommend to him our work "Die psychologischen Errungenschaften Nietzsches" (Barth, Leipzig). Here only this one remark: Nietzsche shows that knowledge of essence is impossible unless we have first seen through and dissolved all the self-deceptions with which humanity, seduced by spirit for millennia, has armored itself against the admission of the violation of life. He calls upon us to become surgeons of our own soul, and presses into our hand the knife that cuts to the very marrow of character. — To Nietzsche's psychological discoveries there is now joined, partly furthered by them, a theory of life (biology) that energetically renounces mechanism, whose by far most significant representative, Melchior Palágyi, in his "Naturphilosophische Vorlesungen," carries through with strict conceptual rigor the separation of spirit and life. — The provisional conclusion, finally, is offered by our own work "Die Grundlagen der Charakterkunde." The voices still ring out discordantly and confusedly intermingled; the one reliable guidance has not yet been granted the rank due to it. To this is added that countless specialized workers, e.g. many neurologists, have indeed perspicaciously unearthed individual findings, but for lack of familiarity with what has in fact already been achieved have, so to speak, missed the connection, erecting makeshift structures that collapse one after another. A treatise would be needed to sift through this critically. Finally, we may recall the book by Prinzhorn, "Leib — Seele — Einheit" (in this series), which has made precisely this sifting its chief task. Only one remark do we wish not to suppress in closing: relatively the most promising of all specialized characterological labors appear to us to be the attempts of the anthropologists oriented toward racescience, whose forefather, Gobineau, has just been cited.
